intro: The DevOps track showed you the GitOps idea and a first Argo CD Application. This lesson opens the `argoproj/argo-cd` repository itself: which process does what, how a sync is ordered, how one ApplicationSet replaces fifty hand-written Applications, how projects fence teams in, and which knobs matter when Argo CD manages hundreds of apps across many clusters.
objectives: Name the Argo CD components and say which one to look at when a sync is slow, wrong or failing
Order a deployment with sync waves and PreSync, PostSync and SyncFail hooks
Generate Applications per directory or per cluster with an ApplicationSet
Restrict a team to its repositories, clusters and resource kinds with an AppProject
Tune and shard the application controller for large installations

sections.heading: Inside the repository: one binary, several jobs

blocks.text: Argo CD is written in Go and ships as one container image whose entrypoint decides which component to run. The top-level folders of the repository map almost one-to-one onto the processes you see in the `argocd` namespace, which makes the code a useful map when you debug.

rows: gRPC/REST API behind the UI and CLI: auth, RBAC, sync and rollback requests, Git webhooks
Clones Git (or pulls Helm and OCI charts), caches them, and renders plain manifests
Compares live state with rendered desired state, sets sync and health status, runs syncs
Turns one ApplicationSet into many Applications using generators
Sends Slack, email or webhook messages on triggers such as sync failed
Optional: writes rendered manifests back to Git for the source hydrator

blocks.text: Two more pieces complete the picture: **Redis**, a cache the controller and API server share (it holds no state you cannot rebuild), and **Dex**, an optional identity broker for SSO. The `gitops-engine/` folder holds the reusable diff-and-sync library that the controller is built on, and `resource_customizations/` holds the Lua health checks that teach Argo CD when a custom resource counts as Healthy.

Debug by component. Manifests look wrong or a Helm value is ignored: read the **repo server** logs. Status stuck at Unknown or syncs queue up: the **application controller**. Login, RBAC or webhook problems: the **API server**.

sections.heading: How a sync is ordered: phases, waves and hooks

blocks.text: A sync is not one big `kubectl apply`. Argo CD runs it in **phases** — PreSync, Sync, PostSync, plus SyncFail if something breaks — and inside each phase it applies resources in **waves**. A wave is the integer in the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation. Everything defaults to wave 0, waves can be negative, and Argo CD applies the lowest wave first and waits for it to be healthy before moving on.

A **hook** is any resource carrying the `argocd.argoproj.io/hook` annotation, usually a Job. A PreSync hook that fails stops the sync before your Deployment is touched, which makes it the right place for a database migration or a pre-flight check. PostSync hooks run only after every resource is Healthy, so they suit smoke tests and notifications.

blocks.caption: A migration Job that must finish before the new pods roll out
blocks.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: ghcr.io/example/orders:1.8.0
          command: ["./manage", "migrate"]

items: Put a Namespace, CRDs or a Secret in wave `-1` so they exist before the workloads in wave 0 that need them.
When pruning, the order is reversed: higher waves are deleted first.
Hooks do not run during a selective sync (syncing only some resources from the UI).

blocks.text: Once you have a dozen services or clusters, hand-writing one Application each turns into copy-paste drift. An **ApplicationSet** pairs a **generator**, which produces a list of parameter sets, with a **template** that becomes one Application per parameter set. The generators in the docs include List, Cluster, Git (directories or files), Matrix and Merge (combine two generators), Pull Request, SCM Provider, Cluster Decision Resource and Plugin.

blocks.caption: One Application per folder under addons/: add a folder, get an app
blocks.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: cluster-addons
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/example/platform.git
        revision: HEAD
        directories:
          - path: addons/*
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{.path.basename}}'
    spec:
      project: platform
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/example/platform.git
        targetRevision: HEAD
        path: '{{.path.path}}'
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: '{{.path.basename}}'
      syncPolicy:
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true

blocks.text: The Cluster generator is the multi-cluster workhorse: it emits one parameter set per cluster registered in Argo CD, optionally filtered by label, so `env=prod` clusters get the production overlay automatically. Matrix a Cluster generator with a Git generator and you get every add-on on every matching cluster from about thirty lines of YAML.

Deleting an ApplicationSet deletes the Applications it generated, and with the resources finalizer those delete their workloads too. Review ApplicationSet changes as carefully as you would a production deploy.

Every Application belongs to an **AppProject**, and the `default` project allows everything. For anything shared, create one project per team that says which repositories it may deploy from, which cluster and namespace pairs it may deploy to, and which resource kinds it may create. A team that cannot create a ClusterRole through Argo CD cannot escalate its own permissions through Git either.

blocks.caption: The payments team may deploy its own repos into payments-* namespaces only
blocks.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/example/payments-*
  destinations:
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: payments-*
  clusterResourceWhitelist: []
  namespaceResourceBlacklist:
    - group: ''
      kind: ResourceQuota

blocks.text: An empty `clusterResourceWhitelist` means no cluster-scoped resources at all. Projects also carry roles whose JWT tokens let a CI job trigger syncs for that project only, and **sync windows** that block automatic syncs during, say, a quarter-end freeze.

By default the controller re-checks Git for every Application about every three minutes (`timeout.reconciliation` in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap) and handles work with 20 status processors and 10 operation processors. The high-availability guide suggests about 50 and 25 for roughly a thousand applications. Configure Git webhooks so a push triggers a refresh at once instead of waiting for the next poll.

items: **Shard the controller** when it manages many clusters: raise the replica count of `argocd-application-controller` and set `ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS` to the same number; clusters are spread across replicas.
**Scale the repo server** horizontally when rendering is the bottleneck, which is common with large Helm charts or many Kustomize overlays.
Use the HA manifests (Redis with Sentinel, multiple API servers) for production, and pin a released version instead of tracking `stable`.
Install with `kubectl apply --server-side`: some CRDs, such as ApplicationSet, exceed the annotation size limit of client-side apply.

blocks.text: Newer releases add the **source hydrator** (beta since v3.5): instead of rendering Helm or Kustomize in memory, Argo CD renders once, commits the plain manifests to a branch, and syncs from there, so every change to what actually runs is a reviewable diff. It is disabled by default and needs the commit server.

practice.title: Waves, hooks and an ApplicationSet on a laptop cluster
steps: Create a local cluster with kind or k3d, then install Argo CD with `kubectl create namespace argocd` and `kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts -f` pointing at the install.yaml of a pinned release.
Run `kubectl get pods -n argocd` and match each pod to a folder in the table above.
In a Git repo of your own, create `addons/nginx` and `addons/redis` folders with a simple Deployment in each, then apply the ApplicationSet from this lesson pointing at your repo.
Run `argocd app list` and confirm two Applications appeared; add an `addons/echo` folder, push, and watch a third one appear.
Add a PreSync Job that runs `sleep 20` and a ConfigMap annotated with sync-wave `-1`, sync, and watch the order in the UI's sync status panel.
Make the Job fail (`exit 1`) and confirm the Deployment is not updated.
Delete the ApplicationSet in a throwaway cluster and observe what happens to the generated Applications.

focus: Repo server renders manifests; application controller diffs and syncs; API server serves the UI, CLI and webhooks.
Sync order is phase (PreSync, Sync, PostSync) then wave (lowest integer first, default 0).
A failed PreSync hook stops the sync before workloads change: put migrations and checks there.
ApplicationSet = generator (list of parameters) + template (one Application each).
Never leave teams on the default project; restrict repos, destinations and kinds with an AppProject.
Scale by sharding the controller across clusters and adding repo server replicas.

items.desc: All Applications with sync and health status
Show what a sync would change
Sync now and delete resources removed from Git
Roll back to a history entry (auto-sync must be off)
Register another cluster from your kubeconfig
Run before the main sync (also Sync, PostSync, SyncFail, Skip)
Delete the previous hook before creating the new one
Auto-sync, delete removed resources, revert manual drift
Create the destination namespace if missing
Use server-side apply for large or shared objects
Ignore fields another controller owns, such as HPA replicas
argocd-cm: how often apps re-check Git
Must equal the controller replica count when sharding
argocd-cmd-params-cm: turn on the source hydrator (beta)

pitfalls: Leaving everything in the `default` project, so any repo can deploy anything anywhere.
Fighting the HPA: Argo CD resets `replicas` on every sync unless you drop it from Git or add an ignoreDifferences rule.
Relying on three-minute polling instead of configuring Git webhooks, then wondering why deploys lag.
Deleting an ApplicationSet or an Application with the resources finalizer and taking production down with it.
Tracking the `stable` manifests in production instead of pinning a release.

quiz.q: An Application shows the wrong image tag even though the Helm values file in Git is correct. Which component's logs should you read first?
options: The repo server, which renders the Helm chart into manifests
The notifications controller, which sends sync messages
Redis, which stores the desired state for each Application
Dex, which brokers single sign-on for the user interface
quiz.explain: The repo server is the component that renders Helm, Kustomize or plain YAML into manifests; a value being ignored is a rendering problem. Redis is only a rebuildable cache.

quiz.q: You need a schema migration to finish before new pods start, and the deploy must stop if the migration fails. What do you use?
options: A Job annotated as a PreSync hook
A Job annotated as a PostSync hook
A Job placed in sync-wave 10
A Job excluded with Prune=false
quiz.explain: A PreSync hook runs before the main sync phase, and if it fails the sync stops before workloads are updated. PostSync runs after everything is healthy, which is too late.

quiz.q: Your platform repo has one folder per add-on and you add new add-ons every month. Which approach avoids writing a new Application each time?
options: An ApplicationSet with a Git directory generator
One Application pointing at the repository root
A PostSync hook that runs kubectl apply
An AppProject with a wildcard source repo
quiz.explain: The Git directory generator emits one parameter set per matching folder and the template turns each into an Application, so a new folder becomes a new app automatically.

quiz.q: A team's Application tries to create a ClusterRole and the sync is refused. Their AppProject has `clusterResourceWhitelist: []`. Why?
options: An empty whitelist allows no cluster-scoped resources
ClusterRoles can only be created by Argo CD admins via the CLI
The repo server cannot render RBAC objects
Sync waves must be negative for RBAC resources
quiz.explain: The project's cluster resource whitelist lists the cluster-scoped kinds it may create; an empty list means none, which stops teams escalating permissions through Git.

quiz.q: One Argo CD instance manages 40 clusters and the application controller keeps running out of memory. What is the documented fix?
options: Shard the controller: more replicas with ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS set to match
Add more Redis replicas so the cache holds more clusters
Lower timeout.reconciliation so each check finishes sooner
Add API server replicas behind the load balancer
quiz.explain: Controller sharding spreads clusters across controller replicas, so each holds only part of the cluster state in memory. Redis and the API server do not do the diffing.
